Outline: Divide the polynomials first, decompose the proper fraction that remains into partial fractions, and then integrate term by term.
Step 1 — Long division
Since the degree of the numerator is greater than the degree of the denominator we need to use long division to get a simpler form to express

\[ {{CT:0}}. \]

Using long division we get that

\[ {{CT:0}} = {{CT:2}} + {{CT:3}} \]

Step 2 — Partial fractions
Partial fractions: \( \frac{p(x)}{(x-a)(x-b)}=\frac{A}{x-a}+\frac{B}{x-b} \); a repeated factor \( (x-a)^2 \) gives \( \frac{A}{x-a}+\frac{B}{(x-a)^2} \); an irreducible \( x^2+bx+c \) gives \( \frac{Ax+B}{x^2+bx+c} \)
Now,

\[ {{CT:2}} = {{CT:4}}{{CT:5}} + {{CT:6}}{{CT:7}} \]

So, multiplying by {{CT:8}} both sides we get

\[ \begin{aligned} {{CT:9}} &= {{CT:10}} + {{CT:11}} \\ &= {{CT:12}} \end{aligned} \]

So, equating coefficients in {{CT:13}} we get that a system of equations that can be solved to get \(A = {{CT:14}}\) and \(B = {{CT:15}}\)
Step 3 — Integrating term by term
Hence,

\[ {{CT:0}} = {{CT:16}} \]

So,

\[ \begin{aligned} \int {{CT:0}} d{{CT:1}} &= \int {{CT:16}} d{{CT:1}} \\ &= {{CT:14}} \int {{CT:5}} d{{CT:1}} {{CT:15}} \int {{CT:7}} d{{CT:1}} + \int ({{CT:3}}) d{{CT:1}} \\ &= {{CT:17}} {{CT:18}} + {{CT:19}}+c \\ &= {{CT:20}}+c \end{aligned} \]
